author: timneutkens
text:
Update: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/37136#discussioncomment-3978551

---


This RFC outlines the biggest update to Next.js since it was introduced in 2016:

- **Nested Layouts:** Build complex applications with nested routes.
- **Designed for Server Components:** Optimized for subtree navigation.
- **Improved Data Fetching:** Fetch in layouts while avoiding waterfalls.
- **Using React 18 Features:** Streaming, Transitions, and Suspense.
- **Client and Server Routing:** Server-centric routing with _SPA-like_ behavior.
- **100% incrementally adoptable**: No breaking changes so you can adopt gradually.
- **Advanced Routing Conventions**: Offscreen stashing, instant transitions, and more.

[👉 Read the RFC](https://nextjs.org/blog/layouts-rfc) – we'd love to hear your feedback and comments.

author: SferaDev
text:
According to the RFC, "by default, files inside app will be rendered on the server as React Server Components". And in server components we will be able to directly fetch data and interact with a db or any external API directly from the React code (as showcased in the original RSC demo with the react-pg or react-fs example libraries).

However, instead of fetching data in the component itself (either a layout or a page), in the RFC it looks like the recommendation would still be to use getServerSideProps as in the current SSR pages.

Would there be a difference between choosing one method or the other? Will the "use server code directly in React" be discouraged in Next?

If we choose to directly call server code in React, how can we tell Next that it should or shouldn't make it a static route? Will the server code defined in the component be able to run statically too (without using getStaticProps)?

If we call server code in the component level, can we still share it with parent/children segment layouts? Will there be a route context or similar that can be used to read/refresh data from any part of the tree (including a client component)?

I definitely see a window for database providers and APIs publish React utilities either in the form of hooks ([like Hydrogen's useShopQuery](https://shopify.dev/api/hydrogen/hooks/global/useshopquery)) or components ([like the experimental proof of concept from prisma](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/tree/main/packages/react-prisma)).

At this early stage and without having read the second post yet, it looks like building this kind of tooling on top of React RSC will probably be limited and adoption reduced if getServerSideProps/getStaticProps are still the recommended way of providing data to a route.

Note: Before reading the RFC I had naively thought that getServerSideProps would be deprecated in favor of data fetching in RSC, so I might be a little biased against it with my "how would I do it" expectations.

Also, I was about to submit some RFC related to this. Expand to see it:

<details>

# RFC: Routes Directories

## ****Goals****

- High cohesion between files.
- Deduce file entropy.
- Colocation of non-routable files.

## Non-Goals

- Prescribe directory structure inside the routes directory beside reserved files.

## Background

At the moment, all files under the `pages` directory define a routable URL (except the reserved files such as `_middleware.js`).

When one of those page files becomes too big, developers would extract the content into files **outside** the `pages` directory because of the limitation that every file is a routable URL since they are not routable files.

Mostly increases drastically the entropy, and cohesion because they are no way to colocate the files, colocating the files far away from their usage. Or sometimes end up replicating the same `pages` directory outside the `pages` directory to make sense of the files outside of it.

As the application code base grow such problem become more predominant, especially combined with scaling a team. It is not clear what goes where, and which pages use some of the files without relaying of searches or some sort of tooling that would give you such information.

A way we solve this was by adopting the following ADR: [https://github.com/straw-hat-team/adr/tree/master/adrs/5541831634#routes-directory-structure](https://github.com/straw-hat-team/adr/tree/master/adrs/5541831634#routes-directory-structure)

Particularly the “Routes Directory Structure” section which was added to solve such a problem.

## Proposal

- Routes segments **MUST** be defined by adding `routes` directory (subject to change, maybe `pages`, the reason we prefer the `routes` name is that we leverage such naming in React-Native or any other Renderers using React toolkit) with a subdirectory representing the route segment where the `index.js` file under such route segment subdirectory represent the loadable entry for such route segment.
- All reserved files could be repeatable as a direct child of the route segment subdirectory under `routes` directory.

Example:

```
URL: http://acme.io/authors/articles
<rootDir>
└── app
    └── routes
        └── authors
            ├── index.tsx
            └── routes
                └── articles
                    └── index.tsx
```

```
URL: http://acme.io/authors/articles/:articleId/
<rootDir>
└── app
    └── routes
        └── authors
            ├── index.tsx
            └── routes
                └── articles
                    ├── index.tsx
                    └── routes
                        └── [articleId]
                            ├── layout.js
                            └── index.tsx
```

### Notes

Another guideline that we have is that you can only import from higher or sibling directories and files. Because you can not share code as a direct child of `routes` directories, all the shared resources for a given route segment will meet somewhere where it would follow such a guideline. You should be able to tell from the file-system tree which directories may be using what.

The reason that is so important is that in code reviews, and whatnot; you can assess how critical the changes may be, the higher in the tree, the more risky changes become because they would affect many things. The lower you are in the tree, the more freedom you could have since the code is more isolated.

## Downsides

- One more extra directory to create.

## Implementation

Introduce some `experimental.newRouting` config in the `next.config.js` that allows such directory strategy.

</details>

I completely share this point, being able to opt-in in serial (waterfall) data-fetching is important. In serial mode, the nested `getServerSideProps()` should be able to access data fetched in a parent `getServerSideProps()` (using the existing `GetServerSidePropsContext` object?).

One approach I thought about would be to have a specific methods for such serial data-fetching, for example:
- `getServerSideProps`: works as explained in the RFC, i.e. all data-fetching are done in parallel:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2678610/169969910-e8a21cb2-9072-4bb6-a7d9-73ba6d51c031.png)
- `getBlockingServerSideProps` (or any other more meaningful name): if a layout implements it, the data-fetching is sequential and nested segments data-fetching methods need to wait for it. The result of this function should be accessible to the nested segments methods as well. This would basically work as on the left side of the above image.

`getBlockingServerSideProps()` should also be able to interrupt the rendering and data-fetching of the rest of the page when needing to redirect for example.

author: ValentinH
text:
One use-case I have in mind is about dealing with JWT authentication and Refresh tokens. 
Today, in our application, we have a `withAuthentication()` function that we use to wrap the `getServerSideProps()` of pages that require authentication.
In this function, we deal with cookies to verify that the user is logged-in and if the access token is valid and still active. If the access token has expired and there is a refresh token available, we need to refresh the access token. This means regenerating a new token by checking that the refresh token is valid and matching a user, setting the new access token in the response cookies and also pass the new access token to the wrapped `getServerSideProps()` so that it can use it to authenticate when doing API calls (remote GraphQL API in our case).

With the current state of the RFC regarding parallel data-fetching, I feel like all segments `getServerSideProps` of a given page would need to handle the refresh token logic. Instead, we should only do it once in the first layout requiring authentication.

author: colinclerk
text:
Auth for parallel loading can definitely be a headache. But, I don't believe `getBlockingServerSideProps` is strictly necessary.  An alternative design can leverage a 307 redirect.

Let's use the request from the illustration as an example: **/dashboard/settings**

When the request comes in, `getServerSideProps` runs simultaneously in DashboardLayout and SettingsPage.

Let's say SettingsPage receives an expired JWT and throws an error to cancel it's rendering.

And, let's say DashboardLayout does three things:
1. Refreshes the JWT
2. Issues a Set-Cookie header with the new JWT
3. Issues a 307 redirect to `req.path` (effectively retrying the same request, this time with the updated cookie)

When the retry request is received, the JWT is updated and your `withAuthentication` function will work fine across all `getServerSideProps`.

---

This same design works for "protected routes".  Let's look at the same request to **/dashboard/settings**, but assume there is no JWT instead of an expired JWT.

SettingsPage receives no JWT and throws an error.

DashboardLayout receives no JWT and issues a 301 redirect to **/sign-in**, where the user can sign in.

---

This is moreorless how Clerk solved this problem for Remix, which faces the same challenges.

The solution depends on two things:
1. DashboardLayout has a way of issuing a redirect and setting a cookie from its getServerSideProps
2. The throw in SettingsPage doesn't supersede the redirect in DashboardLayout.

author: timneutkens
text:
Rendering of components happens on the server, these components are not sent to the browser to render there, however React knows how to apply the rendered components output client-side.

I guess the best way to explain it is comparing it to how Next.js client-side routing works today. Note that I'm intentionally not mentioning prefetching in the story to simplify / make it easier to understand the flow without optimization:

1. You click `<Link href="/dashboard">`
2. JavaScript entrypoint for `/dashboard` is loaded which includes all components to render that page, including components that might only be shown based on certain props and such
3. At the same time a request to the server is made for the getServerSideProps or getStaticProps result. You can see this in the network tab as `/_next/data/<buildid>/dashboard.json`
4. Once both the JS and data is loaded the components are rendered client-side

With the changes in the RFC it becomes somewhat like this:

1. You click `<Link href="/dashboard">`
2. A request to the server is made for the `/dashboard` React render instructions (for lack of a better word), it can be compared to the data request mentioned above, except instead of running `getServerSideProps` it ends up data fetching and rendering server-side (Server Components) and returning the rendered React components
3. The "React render instructions" are executed in the browser and render out the html

There's a few fundamental differences between the two approaches:
- In the new model you don't need to load JS in the browser to do a client-side navigation. The only client-side code loaded is React/ReactDOM and the Next.js router. Note that the Next.js router will be smaller than it is today as it mostly wires up React features.
- The request to the server leverages the new streaming protocol to allow starting the render even before all data is loaded, this means that you'll be able to model loading states without having to ship the JS for the loading state to the browser.

On top of this there's additional optimizations the RFC unlocks like rendering down from the common layout instead of rendering the whole page on the server, this makes it different from navigation using `<a>` (and even client-side navigation in Next.js today) as it avoids loading the JS runtime again, it also avoids rendering the whole page as it can re-render only a small part of the page if at least one layout is shared.

Has the term "wrapper" (or a similar generic name) been considered instead of layouts? It was mentioned by @cassidoo on https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/26389 and this is also how I've been calling mine in my Next projects. Many times my pages are wrapped in other things than just "layouts", which is quite a limiting term.

Here is an example of how I've been using the page property pattern in my projects:

```jsx
SettingsPage.getWrappers = page => (
  <LoggedInOnly>
    <SomeLibProvider>
      <DashboardLayout>
        {page}
      </DashboardLayout>
    </SomeLibProvider>
  </LoggedInOnly>
);
```

I like this pattern because it allows me to declare a whole bunch of nested wrappers **outside of the page component**. Any level of nesting (indentation) removed from the page component is an improvement on readability, and helps avoiding gigantic blocks of JSX. Of course it's always possible to create some kind of wrapping component ourselves around the page, but I find it less elegant than the `getWrappers` solution I am currently using, and it would remount on page changes.

The term layout is very tied to rendering a UI container, and any wrapper that is not specifically about UI (like `LoggedInOnly` or `SomeLibProvider` would seem out of place if put in a `layout.js` file.

I would be happy to keep a `layout.js` file only for UI stuff, but also have some way to nest-wrap my pages with other kinds of wrappers in something like `wrappers.js`. But having both `layout.js` and `wrappers.js` seems redundant. And having only `wrappers.js` is less explicit when only dealing with layout wrappers. So not sure what to propose here, but thought it was worth having this conversation.

author: sebmarkbage
text:
This proposal is a little different than just getLayout or getWrappers because inside each layout each nested layout/page is "keyed" with a unique key. This means that each layout surrounding its page is shared between multiple pages but each page doesn't share identity/state and each sibling layout above it doesn't shared identity/state. See [the discussion above](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/37136#discussioncomment-2814789) for a similar topic.

This opens up for other potential wrappers. For example, one idea I've had is for a `template.js` that behaves like `layout.js` but it goes inside the layout - inside the key. This means that each template.js would be a "copy" - a new instance - for each page or nested layout within it. That can be useful as a convenience for creating shared containers around each page but that for example animate between containers instead of animating the content of the containers.

In other words, there are more than one type of wrapper so using a more generic terminology here is actually a downside since it doesn't let us add new ones and call them the group all together as something more generic.

But what if I had a route that's significant enough to have a different, special url, and still wanted to use the admin/dashboard nested layout? That would get verbose very quickly.

I think nuxt does this a tad better by having a layout field in the sfc config (although they use a string which is bad). I think a layout or getLayout export from the page file would work best. That'd work similar to how community layout functionality implementations work now. Naturally, to have the layouts preserve state between components, they would have to be the same reference wise, i.e. would have to be defined seperately.

One of the popular vite ssr libraries has a very nice solution similar to the above as well, iirc.

Tldr, I just don't think tightly coupling an advanced system like this with the simplicity of the file system is such a good idea, personally.

author: corysimmons
text:
### Suggestion for the concern people have about 50 `layout.jsx` and `page.jsx` files breaking cmd+p and making all your editor tabs look identical.

```
- app
	- layout.jsx
	- dashboard
		- DashboardLayout.jsx
		- package.json
		- settings
			- SettingsPage.jsx
			- package.json
	- banana
		- layout.jsx
		- subbanana
			- page.jsx
```

**`app/dashboard/package.json`**
```json
{
  "main": "./DashboardLayout.jsx" 
}
```

**`app/dashboard/settings/package.json`**
```json
{
  "main": "./SettingsPage.jsx" 
}
```

This is how I fix this problem when co-locating component stuff in **large projects** and it **works great**.

**Example:**

```js
- components
	- Button
		- Button.tsx
		- Button.styles.ts
		- Button.container.ts
		- Button.test.ts
		- package.json // { "main": "./Button.tsx" }
```

I would also suggest adding a mapper to `next.config.js` so people can automate this pattern (and not clutter their file structure with a bunch of single-purpose `package.json` files).

Something like:

**next.config.js**
```js
const { capitalize } = require('lodash')

module.exports = {
  // ...
	mapAppPaths: ({ parentDirName }) => ({
		layouts: `${capitalize(parentDirName)}Layout.tsx`,
		pages: `${capitalize(parentDirName)}Page.tsx`,
	}),
}
```

>**Disclaimer:** I only briefly skimmed the RFC and haven't looked at this thread at all.

Credit to @alejalapeno for showing me that cool `package.json` technique.

author: corysimmons
text:
Using `package.json`'s [`main` field](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v8/configuring-npm/package-json#main) as it's intended (as something that tells Node _"this is the project/folder's entrypoint"_) actually leans into exactly what core Node is expecting so lots of things like  `import`s being simpler (e.g. `import AppLayout from './app'` instead of `import AppLayout from './app/AppLayout'`), hyperclick, and other tooling, just play nice together.

Having an extra `package.json` in a component folder can seem bloaty if there's just a single file in a dir, but it isn't noticeable if there are a lot of files in a dir.

```js
- components
	- Logo
		- Logo.tsx
		- Logo.test.ts
		- package.json // 👈
	- Button
		- Button.tsx
		- Button.test.ts
		- package.json // 👈 Slight smell, but not bad & it's easy for people to adopt
		               //    (later they'd just use the next.config.js mapper and simply remove all these in a single commit)
- app
	- AppLayout.tsx
	- AppLayout.test.ts
	- package.json
	- dashboard
		- DashboardLayout.tsx
		- DashboardLayout.test.ts
		- package.json
		- settings
			- SettingsPage.tsx
			- SettingsPage.test.ts
			- package.json
			- components
				- Input
					- Input.tsx
					- Input.module.css
					- Input.test.ts
					- package.json // 👈 Blends in with all the other co-located files
		- search
			- SearchPage.tsx
			- SearchPage.test.ts
			- package.json
```

I take your point though, and I think there would have to be some way to obfuscate this from the dev's point of view, but not from Node's, which is why I suggested the mapping config in `next.config.js`

**Same structure with that `next.config.js` tweak:**

```js
- components
	- Logo
		- Logo.tsx
		- Logo.test.ts
	- Button
		- Button.tsx
		- Button.test.ts
- app
	- AppLayout.tsx
	- AppLayout.test.ts
	- dashboard
		- DashboardLayout.tsx
		- DashboardLayout.test.ts
		- settings
			- SettingsPage.tsx
			- SettingsPage.test.ts
			- components
				- Input
					- Input.tsx
					- Input.module.css
					- Input.test.ts
		- search
			- SearchPage.tsx
			- SearchPage.test.ts
```

☝️ This is the absolute smallest amount of files you'd need to solve the _"every file is called `layout` or `page`"_ problem.

author: ghost
text:
Love this discussion! Yeah my use-case using another framework was a bit different. Basically, we had to show different routes depending on what access the user has. If they didn't have admin access, but they attempted to access an admin route, we'd just redirect them to a 404 page. On every nested route that used a loader we would add a call to the `/me` route. On nested routes, we had to call the `/me` route to grab the user's role/features. There's an obvious argument that could be made here where we'd just store the claims in JWT token and in order to get the newest claims the user would need to logout and log back in or refresh their auth token, but **I really just wanted the loader to make a request at the parent route and then provide that data to child loaders.**

Some other solutions I looked into: potentially using a request cache so that for the same request the loaders could race to create the promise and then the promise would be awaited. The problem was that there was no way of distinguishing the request from another, and I didn't want there to be request collisions between users (the system was multi-tenant so this would have been REALLY bad). I also looked into adding some kind of request ID but I would have needed to make some bigger changes. And another solution I looked into was a server-side cache of some sort, potentially using Redis, but again super heavy-handed and then we had the problem of having to invalidate that cache somehow.

Anyhow I gave up on that framework and just went back to plain old CSR.

> The current RFC does not mitigate the main issue raised by the community: the lack of component-level data fetching. It's clearly a good step towards that with goodies like the state of the page being preserved on navigation.

Component-level data fetching is a step further from this RFC but in order to achieve it you'll still need the changes in the RFC are still needed to cover things like navigating between pages while showing a loading state. Specifically suspense for data fetching is not stable yet hence why component-level data fetching is not covered in the RFC.

You can read more about the data fetching here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/37136#discussioncomment-2811618

> Nested components (with component-level data fetching) could substitute most of what was expressed under the proposal.

It would only solve one small part of it, as it would mean we'd have to render the full tree on navigation. You can learn more about that difference here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/37136#discussioncomment-2812651

author: timneutkens
text:
> I thought this was all tied to RSC being stable but good to get this is independent of that

Suspense for data fetching is more so a complementary feature on top of Server Components. Server Components is specifically about rendering components on the server (or during build) and using the rendered result during client-side navigation / hydration so that you don't need to ship components to the browser. You can read more about that here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/37136#discussioncomment-2812651

    layout.js
    \posts
      page.js

author: vwkd
text:
@leerob I don't think it's a good idea to collocate other files in the `app` folder that are not creating a route. You'd probably have multiple such files, so you'd probably want to allow folders to organize them. But then those folders create routes, so you’d need to allow folders that don’t create routes. So you’d either restrict them by a special name like a leading underscore, which then creates issues if you want to use that special name in a route. Alternatively you decide based on if there is a leaf `page.js` somewhere in a subfolder. Both options, especially the latter, make it harder to figure out which routes exist, because you have to parse out the folders which aren’t routes.

I’d prefer to have a `routes` folder which can only contain routes and other stuff only outside of it.

author: alex-krasikau
text:
Hey there, thanks for the blog post!

I have a few edge cases from my experience that would be really nice to handle with a new Layout implementation.

1. Having a huge number of pages that are mostly client-side rendered. In my case I have 10000 game pages that render mostly client-side in the iframe and take only `name` from the CMS.

So, if I use dynamic routes approach with `/catalog/games/[gameSlug]` route, then I face a number of issues right away, that makes it impossible to use:
- 10000 heavy layout content requests
- 10000 small game content requests
- 10000 full page renders

1.1. From what I see, new layout feature solves first issue, cause it makes a single request for layout and reuse it across all the child routes.

1.2. To solve the second issue can be introduced new hook, similar to `getStaticPaths` by nature, that allows making single batch request for the content (or several chunks requests for 10000 entities). I haven’t tested it yet, but I think that it’s still doable with a Data Loader even with the current implementation.

1.3. Is it possible to cache parent layout to only render game content part and merge results to avoid 10000 heavy renders?

2. There’s an alternative to this approach, I don’t really see a lot of impact of using static rendering in this case, cause loading single field (or small amount of content) makes no sense when we create such a huge load on the build server. So it would be nice if we can still use next.js routing system and mark some pages as client rendered.

As I can’t use static rendering because of provided reasons, if forces me out of the next.js dynamic routing system and I have to switch to `/catalog/games?gameSlug=`.

Another case is when we have two dynamic parts in the URL and one of them is not available during build time. Here’s an example from the exported application that uses own implementation of the localization: `/[locale]/catalog/category/[categorySlug]`. From the requirements of the application we don't know the category before build and it's, let's say, built based on user input. So once I set this structure, I can't use `export` anymore.

So I propose adding an extra flag to the page like `export const rendering = "client"`. So Next.js can understand that this page has dynamic structure and page layout that depends on static content can be rendered by the parent layout component.

This way we can continue using next.js dynamic routing and offload some routes from rendering build time and being able to `export` the application.

author: timneutkens
text:
Given that this question has come up a bunch in this thread I'm going to share how this will work even though it'll be in part 2 of the RFC:

```
app
├── layout.js // renders <html> / <head> / <body>
├── (main)
│   ├── layout.js
│   ├── dashboard
│   │   └── page.js
│   └── settings
│       └── page.js
├── (login)
│   ├── layout.js
│   └── login
│       └── page.js
└── (other)
    ├── layout.js
    └── checkout
        └── page.js
```

The `()` syntax can be used to create "route groups" which are not part of the URL and allow you to create separate layouts for different routes. This gives you full flexibility of what layout will render on a certain path. I modeled the tree based on your example but the `()` syntax can be nested further as well. 

In addition to that it also allows you to create completely separate root layouts:

```
app
├── (main)
│   ├── layout.js // renders <html> / <head> / <body>
│   ├── dashboard
│   │   └── page.js
│   └── settings
│       └── page.js
├── (login)
│   ├── layout.js // renders <html> / <head> / <body>
│   └── login
│       └── page.js
└── (other)
    ├── layout.js // renders <html> / <head> / <body>
    └── checkout
        └── page.js
```

Hope that clarifies the question regarding opting out of layouts for a certain route.

Another benefit of this is that it allows you to group routes by feature:

```
app
├── layout.js // renders <html> / <head> / <body>
└── (dashboard)
    ├── layout.js
    └── dashboard
        ├── page.js
        ├── (billing)
        │   ├── billing
        │   │   └── page.js
        │   ├── creditcard
        │   │   └── page.js
        │   └── invoices
        │       └── page.js
        └── (teams)
            └── team
                ├── page.js
                └── invite
                    └── page.js
```


And because colocation of components is now possible you could essentially have all code/tests/styles for e.g. the `teams` / `billing` pages in that same directory.

author: grzechz
boenrobot
text:
I can think of a workaround for this problem given the current architecture of Nextjs layouts, but I'll admit it feels a bit hacky...

A module that holds your shared data, and provides async getters for it. This module is imported by all files in the layout chain that need the common data, and they call the getter that would otherwise call the data source (be it DB, an HTTP request or whatever your source of truth is) multiple times.

In SSR, the getter call could take the request object, and check it against a WeakMap. If it doesn't exist, set the request as the key in the WeakMap, with the promise for the data as the value. Later, when the same getter is called by another route in the chain, return the promise for that request. Because it is a WeakMap, after the request is handled, the garbage collector should remove the promise from the weak map automatically. From the view point of the caller, they all just await the promise they got from the WeakMap. Whoever calls it first will block on it (while other ones will continue to work until they too need the same data, and then they all wait), and whoever calls it after that will essentially get the data immediately.

You could have multiple different operations stored in the same WeakMap value, stored as an object of named promises, and return the corresponding one based on the getter call, always initializing the "placeholder" object to an empty one when the request object is not an existing key in the WeakMap.

You're sacrificing a tiny bit more memory than you would otherwise (allocating the module and the WeakMap itself), in order to get great speed saving (no second data source lookup + parallel execution where possible) and DX (no passing down of data in a waterfall).

On the client side, the same approach can be used, except that you would not pass a request - just maintain the entire thing as a singleton.

For "bonus points", in both client and server side, you could spawn a worker thread for the actual storage and retrieval. A thin client on the main thread would merely resolve the promise on a message from the worker. That's once again some more memory (for the whole second thread...) for the luxury of letting everything else happen on the main thread at the same time. That last part is essentially what [comlink](https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs/comlink) is for.

author: pjaws
text:
This seems like it will work very well for "apps" where the layout is often defined by the path and known in advance. I'm not clear on how this will work for sites where the layout is dynamic and based on the page or "slug".

On our site, we need to fetch layout data from our CMS on a per-page basis. Most of the time this data is the same from page to page, but it could potentially change even within the same dynamic route. Layouts can also be variable within the same page if an A/B test is active.

It seems like we would need a way to access page props within the Layout component.

author: dtinth
text:
With the current state of the RFC, we’ll have to remember which file names are special to Next.js.

**Here’s a quick quiz: Which of these files are special to Next.js** and which files are custom components that are colocated within the route folder?

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/193136/197685614-94f8df3f-f24b-42c1-b983-427301e1d71b.png)

<details>
<summary>👉  Show answer</summary>

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/193136/197685968-3af3e6a5-578a-4432-84a4-58d81960586b.png)

</details>

Did you get the correct answer?

Also, with the current naming scheme, any new special files that gets added in the future can become a breaking change, if it clashes with pre-existing colocated files.

[SvelteKit resolves this issue by designating a reserved prefix for files that are treated specially by the framework.](https://github.com/sveltejs/kit/discussions/5748#:~:text=The%20%2B%20prefix%20marks%20the%20file%20as%20being%20a%20route%20file) This way that it’s easier for humans to easily tell the difference between colocated files and special files, as text editors will display files with a prefix separately from files without prefix.

[Here’s what the editor file tree will look like if Next.js special files are prefix with `_`.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/193136/197687602-43de1801-f0f2-4e9a-a959-1f093f4c7c16.png)

Sadly, I haven't either. Granted: I haven't scrubbed through all the hours of the nextjs conf footage, but from what I can tell they've not brought anything up.

just to finish fleshing out a thought: I wonder also if a hybrid of this and the previous methodology might work better. (which might be worth putting in it's own post? - unsure - new here).

```
/apps/path/subpath/index.page.js

/apps/path/subpath/index.layout.js

/apps/path/subpath/route.page.js

/apps/path/subpath/deep-path/index.page.js

/apps/path/subpath/deep-path/index.layout.js
```

would become

```
/path/subpath 
--- for which the "page" is /apps/path/subpath/index.page.js and the "layout" is /apps/path/subpath/index.layout.js

/path/subpath/route
--- for which the "page" is /apps/path/subpath/route.page.js and the "layout" is /apps/path/subpath/index.layout.js (since there is no /apps/path/subpath/route.layout.js)

/path/subpath/deep-path
--- for which the "page" is /apps/path/subpath/deep-path/index.page.js and the "layout" is /apps/path/subpath/deep-path/index.layout.js
```

full benefits of the inheritence model that they're going for, better DX for contextual awareness (ie: filenames you're working in), and the `.whatever.js` syntax means how Next.js uses it is semantic.

**Update:** We’re excited to announce [Next.js 13](https://nextjs.org/13), which includes the new `app/` directory (beta) with support for nested layouts, colocation of data fetching, streaming, Server Components by default, and much more.

Inside the `app/` directory, there is a powerful new way to fetch data with React’s `use()` hook and the extended Web `fetch()` API. This allows you to colocate data fetching directly inside components for the most flexibility, including inside layouts.
